title: Provençal Pissaladière with Caramelized Onions, Anchovies & Olives
dek: A crisp, olive-oil-rich rectangular crust carries a generous layer of slow-softened onions, whole anchovy fillets and glossy black olives, matching the unmistakable Provençal tart shown in the finished-dish photograph.
image_alt: Rectangular Provençal pissaladière topped with pale-golden onions, crisscrossed whole anchovy fillets and glossy black olives
ingredients: 3 cups all-purpose flour (360 g), plus up to 2 tbsp only if needed
1 1/2 tsp Diamond Crystal kosher salt, divided
6 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, divided, plus 1 tsp for the bowl
3 lb yellow onions (about 6 medium), halved and sliced 1/4 inch thick
1 tsp fresh thyme leaves or 1/2 tsp dried thyme
2 tins oil-packed anchovy fillets (about 4 oz total), drained to yield 18 to 22 whole fillets
24 pitted Niçoise or Kalamata olives, drained and patted dry

instructions.name: Wake the yeast and mix the olive-oil dough
instructions.text: Stir the warm water, yeast and sugar in a large bowl and stand 5 to 10 minutes, until a creamy foam forms. Add the flour, 1 teaspoon salt and 2 tablespoons olive oil. Stir until no dry flour remains, then knead on a lightly floured counter for 7 to 9 minutes, until smooth and elastic. Add extra flour only a teaspoon at a time if the dough remains wet enough to smear after 3 minutes of kneading.

instructions.name: Let the dough rise while the onions cook
instructions.text: Coat a clean bowl with 1 teaspoon olive oil, turn the dough in it, cover and let rise in a warm, draft-free place for 60 to 75 minutes, until roughly doubled. Begin the onions immediately; their slow cook fits inside most of the rise. If the dough doubles first, gently press it down, cover and refrigerate until the onions are cool enough to use.

instructions.name: Slow-soften the onion topping
instructions.text: Heat 3 tablespoons olive oil in a wide 12-inch heavy skillet or 5-quart Dutch oven over medium-low. Add the onions and remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt. Cook for 45 to 55 minutes, stirring every 4 to 5 minutes and scraping the bottom, until the onions collapse to about 3 cups and turn pale gold with a jammy but not wet texture. Lower the heat if edges brown sharply; the photographed topping is golden, not mahogany.

instructions.name: Season and cool the onions
instructions.text: Stir the garlic, thyme and black pepper into the onions and cook 2 minutes. Spread the mixture on a rimmed plate so it cools quickly and excess steam escapes. It should be warm, not hot, before it meets the risen dough; a steaming topping can soften the crust and restart aggressive yeast activity.

instructions.name: Shape the photographed rectangular base
instructions.text: Set an oven rack in the lower-middle position and heat to 425°F. Brush a 13-by-18-inch rimmed half-sheet pan with the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil. Press and stretch the dough into a roughly 10-by-14-inch rectangle about 1/4 inch thick, leaving a slightly raised rim. If it springs back, wait 10 minutes for the gluten to relax, then finish shaping without tearing it.

instructions.name: Arrange onions, anchovies and olives visibly
instructions.text: Spread the cooled onions evenly to within 1/2 inch of the edge. Lay the whole anchovy fillets diagonally in a loose crisscross pattern, using the visibly irregular lattice in the photograph as the guide rather than hiding or chopping the fish. Place the olives in the open spaces and press them lightly into the onions so they stay put while baking.

instructions.name: Bake until the crust is crisp and golden
instructions.text: Bake at 425°F for 20 to 25 minutes, rotating the pan front to back after 15 minutes, until the raised edge is deep gold, the bottom is crisp and the onions bubble gently around the anchovies. A probe inserted sideways into the bare crust should read about 200°F if visual doneness is uncertain. The anchovies will darken and the olives will wrinkle slightly, as they do in the finished photograph.

instructions.name: Rest, cut and serve
instructions.text: Cool on the pan for 10 minutes so the onion layer settles, then slide the pissaladière onto a board. Cut into 8 lunch-size rectangles or 16 small appetizer squares with a sharp chef's knife or pizza wheel. Serve warm or at room temperature; do not leave it out longer than 2 hours because the moist onion topping and fish should be refrigerated promptly.

why_it_works: A moderately hydrated, olive-oil-enriched yeast dough stays flexible enough to press into a thin rectangle while baking into a crisp base that supports the substantial onion layer.
Cooking three pounds of onions slowly reduces their water and concentrates sweetness without the dark, bitter edges that would conflict with the pale-golden photographed topping.
Cooling the onions before assembly prevents trapped steam from softening the dough and keeps the yeast base from becoming overactive beneath a hot topping.
Whole anchovy fillets arranged above the onions season each piece directly and remain visibly identifiable, while well-drained olives add concentrated briny contrast without extra liquid.
A lower-middle oven rack crisps the oiled bottom as the 425°F heat browns the rim, giving the tart enough structure to cut cleanly after a short rest.
swaps: Use instant yeast in the same quantity and mix it directly with the flour; the water should still be 100–110°F, and the rise may finish 10 to 15 minutes sooner.
Kalamata olives are easier to find than Niçoise olives and keep the same dark, glossy appearance. Rinse very salty olives, then dry them thoroughly before arranging.
For a thicker, breadier base, shape the dough to 9 by 13 inches and add 3 to 5 minutes to the bake. Keep the onion and anchovy quantities unchanged so the topping remains generous.
Oil-cured black olives can replace brined olives, but use 18 because their flavor is more concentrated and remove any pits before serving.

For diners who avoid fish, omit the anchovies and add 1 tablespoon rinsed, chopped capers plus 1/4 teaspoon extra salt to the cooled onions. The result is a useful onion-and-olive tart, but it is not a traditional pissaladière and will not match the photographed anchovy lattice.
storage: Cool completely, cut and refrigerate in a shallow airtight container at 40°F or below for up to 4 days, separating layers with parchment. Reheat pieces on a preheated sheet pan at 375°F for 8 to 12 minutes, until the crust is crisp and the topping reaches 165°F; avoid the microwave when texture matters. Freeze baked, cooled pieces in one layer, then wrap airtight for up to 2 months. Reheat from frozen at 375°F for 15 to 20 minutes. The onion topping can be cooked up to 3 days ahead and refrigerated separately, but bring it close to room temperature before assembling so the dough bakes evenly.
notes: Pissaladière is a savory onion, anchovy and olive specialty associated with Nice and Provence. This yeast-dough version is deliberately distinct from a cheese-topped pizza: there is no tomato sauce or cheese to obscure the three defining toppings.

The CC BY-SA 4.0 photograph was inspected at full size twice. It clearly shows a rectangular golden crust, a thick pale-gold onion layer, whole anchovy fillets in an irregular crisscross and glossy dark olives; the recipe, shaping directions and alt text match those visible elements.

Keep the onion heat low enough that water evaporates before the natural sugars darken. If the pan develops dry brown patches before 35 minutes, add 1 tablespoon water, scrape and reduce the burner rather than adding more oil.

Anchovies and olives vary widely in salinity. The measured salt assumes standard oil-packed anchovies and drained brined olives; taste a cooled spoonful of onion with one small piece of anchovy before adding any extra seasoning.
Calories and cost estimate one-eighth of the dough, onion topping, anchovies, olives and oil. Prices vary most for imported olives and anchovies; small appetizer squares are half a listed serving.

faqs.q: Why is my pissaladière crust soggy under the onions?
faqs.a: The onions were probably still wet or hot. Reduce them until a spoon dragged across the pan leaves a clean path for a moment, spread them on a plate to vent steam, and cool them before assembly. Preheating fully to 425°F and baking on the lower-middle rack also helps the oiled bottom set before the topping can soak in.

faqs.q: Can I make pissaladière ahead for a party?
faqs.a: Yes. Bake it up to 1 day ahead, cool and refrigerate, then reheat uncovered at 375°F for 8 to 12 minutes and serve warm or at room temperature. For a longer head start, cook the onions up to 3 days ahead and make the dough the day before; refrigerate both separately and let the dough soften at room temperature for 45 to 60 minutes before shaping.

faqs.q: Do the anchovies make the finished tart taste aggressively fishy?
faqs.a: They remain distinctly savory and visible, but the sweetness of three pounds of slow-cooked onions and the briny olives balance them. Use good oil-packed fillets, drain them and distribute them evenly so each piece gets a modest amount. Chopping them into the onions would intensify salt throughout and would no longer match the classic visible topping.
